hero.title: The case for giving citizen-built software a governed home.
hero.lead: In a growing number of enterprises the people building working software already outnumber the engineers. Finance analysts, operations managers, support leads and marketers describe what they need to an AI coding tool and get something that runs. The applications are real, they reach real systems, and colleagues depend on them — but none of it was routed through the operating model that governs everything else the business runs on. This is the argument for closing that gap, stage by stage.

executiveSummary.title: One platform. Two groups. Clear governance.
executiveSummary.lead: A governed platform removes the traditional trade-off between speed and control. Builders move fast inside company guardrails. Platform teams keep full visibility and enforceable policy without becoming the bottleneck.

groups.title: Citizen developers
groups.lead: Every new idea no longer requires a specialist queue.
body: Builders work in company-owned source, with company identity and company guardrails from the first commit.
They see the same production logs, errors and traces the platform team sees. They diagnose and propose fixes themselves, then validate the change in a governed preview before it reaches production.
The platform records every action with owner, time and reason. Nothing disappears into shadow IT.

groups.title: Platform administrators
groups.lead: One live inventory replaces fragmented lists.
body: Every asset, its owner, its policy status, its spend and its run history is visible in one place.
Alerts and automated responses surface abnormal consumption or traffic while it is still containable. Agent actions are proposed, reviewed and logged rather than executed unchecked.
Governance effort scales with the number of workloads, not the number of people.

evidence.title: Evidence the logic holds
items: Builders resolve a measurable share of production issues without escalation, because the same evidence is available inside their own workflow.
Abnormal spend and traffic are contained by layered alerts, reporting, rate limiting and egress controls rather than discovered after the bill arrives.
Every deployment carries immutable ownership and audit history, removing the "who owns this and why is it running" problem that grows with headcount.

executiveSummary.footnote: The detailed business case below sets out the full value and risk-mitigated statements for every lifecycle stage, the arguments supporting each one, and the documentation that substantiates them.

audience.title: Who this is for
audience.body: An enterprise where citizen developers — people outside engineering — are already shipping applications, and where that has outgrown the old assumption that everything reaching production passes through an engineering team first. The tell is simple: if the platform group is discovering applications rather than provisioning them, this describes your situation.

structure.title: How the argument is built
structure.body: Six lifecycle stages, from a first prompt through to long-term maintenance. Each stage makes two claims — one about the value a governed platform creates, one about the risk it removes — and each claim is backed by arguments that follow the same chain: what happens today, why it breaks, where it ends, and how it plays out on Vercel. No stage is quantified here; what each argument offers instead is the basis on which your own finance partner would size it.

phases.label: Build
phases.value: Dramatically faster delivery of applications and agents, with approved access to production systems and no setup or technical expertise required from builders.
phases.riskMitigated: Prevents inconsistent architectures, copied credentials, and unsupported code from turning rapid experimentation into security debt and costly rework.

items.title: Approved foundations standardize architecture and controls
items.today: Builders choose their own frameworks, components, security controls, and project structures.
items.problem: Without an approved foundation, every application requires separate architecture, security, accessibility, and maintainability review.
items.impact: Review and remediation grow with application volume, while unfamiliar stacks become expensive to support when ownership changes.
items.withVercel: A maintained application foundation gives every builder approved architecture, controls, and design patterns that improve centrally.
items.quantBasis: Measured from applications created, review and remediation hours avoided, and loaded specialist rate.

items.title: Managed connections keep credentials out of builder workflows
items.today: Builders copy long lived API keys into local files or prompts to connect prototypes to production systems.
items.problem: Once copied, credentials can enter chat history or source control and their use cannot be reliably governed.
items.impact: A useful experiment can create credential rotation, investigation, legal review, service disruption, and lasting security debt.
items.withVercel: Approved runtime connections provide scoped access to production systems without revealing the underlying credentials.
items.quantBasis: Measured from credentials copied per application, incidents avoided, response hours, and the loaded security and legal cost of each.

items.title: Guided delivery removes Git and infrastructure expertise
items.today: Production delivery requires builders to understand repositories, branches, reviews, and infrastructure workflows.
items.problem: The controls intended to govern development become a barrier for people outside engineering.
items.impact: Prototypes remain on laptops or require specialist help, so delivery scales only as fast as scarce engineering capacity.
items.withVercel: Builders create source controlled, deployed applications through guided workflows without operating Git or infrastructure directly.
items.quantBasis: Measured from builder releases, engineering assistance hours avoided, and loaded engineering rate. Compare completion rates before and after.

items.title: Managed integrations remove data and tooling handoffs
items.today: A builder who needs a database, Jira, BigQuery, or Slack must request accounts, credentials, networking, and integration work from specialists.
items.problem: The first backend or tooling dependency breaks self service before the application has proved value.
items.impact: Small workflow ideas stop at demonstration stage or generate recurring work for platform, data, and integration teams.
items.withVercel: Managed integrations connect approved databases and tools like Jira, BigQuery, and Slack through the application workflow — the builder never needs to understand the integration, the credentials, or where the data lives.
items.quantBasis: Measured from integration requests, elapsed days, and specialist hours. Compare time from prototype to a working connected application.

items.title: Company-owned source preserves lineage without specialist seats
items.today: Company policy requires production code in company owned source control, while direct repository access requires paid specialist seats.
items.problem: The company must either buy tools citizen builders do not need or exclude them from the governed source path.
items.impact: Seat costs grow before value is proven, while excluded builders create code with weak ownership and deployment lineage.
items.withVercel: A governed service identity creates company owned source with per user attribution, without requiring direct repository access for every builder.
items.quantBasis: Builders who need source access, the per-seat licence cost avoided for each, and the share of the builder population that would otherwise be excluded from the governed source path.

phases.label: Share
phases.value: One governed platform where teams can securely share working applications, review changes, and give feedback directly in context.
phases.riskMitigated: Prevents employees from using personal accounts, public links, and disconnected tools that leave applications invisible, ungoverned, and impossible to revoke centrally.

items.title: Governed sharing keeps applications private, visible, and revocable
items.today: Builders use personal accounts, public links, screenshots, and unrelated tools because governed sharing is fragmented.
items.problem: Applications, audiences, and ownership cannot be seen or revoked from one place.
items.impact: Sensitive work becomes invisible shadow IT, while fear of exposure prevents useful applications from reaching other teams.
items.withVercel: One governed platform keeps working applications private, company owned, visible, and centrally revocable.
items.quantBasis: Applications shared outside managed accounts; time to identify an owner and revoke access; exposure incidents and remediation cost.

items.title: Protected working previews let stakeholders test every change
items.today: Review happens through screenshots, presentations, or scheduled demonstrations instead of a runnable version of each change.
items.problem: Decision makers cannot test workflows, permissions, responsive behavior, or edge cases themselves.
items.impact: Wrong assumptions survive approval, increasing late rework and reducing trust in builder created software.
items.withVercel: Every change produces a protected working version that approved reviewers can test before release.
items.quantBasis: Measured from review cycles, first feedback latency, defects found after approval, and the rework hours each causes.

items.title: Version-linked feedback removes clarification cycles
items.today: Comments arrive in meetings, messages, and documents without a reliable link to the exact version under review.
items.problem: Builders must interpret ambiguous feedback and reconstruct what the reviewer saw.
items.impact: Clarification cycles delay decisions, reopen defects, and fragment the record of who approved what.
items.withVercel: Reviewers comment directly on the working version, keeping feedback attached to the exact application state.
items.quantBasis: Measured from comments requiring clarification and average delay. Reopened issues; meeting hours replaced by contextual asynchronous review.

phases.label: Deploy
phases.value: Efficient, zero configuration infrastructure that runs applications and agents in production and scales automatically with demand.
phases.riskMitigated: Avoids the cost, specialist staffing, idle capacity, and operational burden of building and managing large Kubernetes environments.

items.title: Managed production removes per-application Kubernetes setup
items.today: Central specialists configure and host each application through infrastructure designed for engineering owned services.
items.problem: Platform tickets, cluster configuration, and per application setup make delivery capacity grow linearly with the estate.
items.impact: At scale, the production queue becomes slower than ungoverned alternatives and valuable applications remain on laptops.
items.withVercel: Infrastructure is derived from the application and company defaults, creating a zero configuration path to production.
items.quantBasis: Measured from applications shipped and platform engineering hours per application, plus value lost during queue time.

items.title: Automatic scaling removes idle capacity without limiting peaks
items.today: Internal applications require standing capacity even though most are rarely used and a few may suddenly reach the whole company.
items.problem: Teams must predict demand before adoption and pay for the long tail of idle services.
items.impact: Under sizing causes outages at the moment of adoption, while over sizing creates a fixed cost floor that grows with application count.
items.withVercel: Automatic scaling adds capacity for bursts and removes traffic cost while applications are idle.
items.quantBasis: Reserved capacity avoided, idle share, peak users served without intervention, and employee hours lost during burst failures.

items.title: One runtime supports interfaces, APIs, background work, and agents
items.today: Interactive interfaces, APIs, background jobs, queues, and long running agent workflows are built and operated as separate services.
items.problem: Each runtime adds architecture, provisioning, monitoring, and specialist ownership before the workflow proves value.
items.impact: Experimental automation creates a permanent worker and queue estate or is implemented unreliably in request handlers.
items.withVercel: Interactive, API, background, and durable work run through one managed production model that charges for active execution.
items.quantBasis: Runtime services eliminated, setup and maintenance hours avoided, and active compute as a share of total workflow duration.

items.title: Immutable releases give every application one recovery point
items.today: Frontends, APIs, and workers ship through separate pipelines with independent versions and recovery procedures.
items.problem: A release can leave incompatible parts live, while rollback requires specialists to reconstruct a known good combination.
items.impact: Partial recovery extends employee downtime, risks repeated work or data errors, and slows future releases.
items.withVercel: The application ships as one immutable deployment with one consistent version and one recovery point.
items.quantBasis: Measured from release incidents caused by version mismatch, restoration time, and affected employee hours. Pipelines eliminated per application.

phases.label: Authenticate
phases.value: Internal applications remain internal, while users access production systems with their existing permissions and credentials stay hidden from builders.
phases.riskMitigated: Prevents public exposure, shared credentials, excessive permissions, and orphaned access from becoming security, legal, compliance, or operational incidents.

items.title: Identity protection is on by default for every application
items.today: Each builder must add access control correctly or anyone with the link can open the application.
items.problem: A mandatory security control depends on every builder remembering and implementing it without error.
items.impact: One omission can expose internal or personal data, while local accounts and one off lists leave access behind after offboarding.
items.withVercel: Company identity protects every application by default, and central identity removal revokes access across the estate.
items.quantBasis: Share protected by company identity, exposure exceptions found, audit hours, and revocation latency after offboarding.

items.title: User identity carries existing permissions into production systems
items.today: Applications query production systems through one shared service identity regardless of which employee initiated the request.
items.problem: The source system sees the application rather than the person, bypassing existing grants and user level audit records.
items.impact: Users may receive data they cannot access directly, turning the application into a privilege escalation path.
items.withVercel: The signed in user’s identity reaches the production system, which applies the permissions it already governs.
items.quantBasis: Sensitive requests carrying end user identity, unauthorized row exposure tests, and custom access logic eliminated per application.

items.title: End-to-end attribution follows consequential actions
items.today: A user signs in, but downstream API calls and agent actions execute under unrelated shared credentials.
items.problem: The identity chain breaks before the query, change, or external action that matters.
items.impact: Investigators cannot attribute actions, and compliance cannot demonstrate least privilege or individual accountability.
items.withVercel: Human and agent actions remain connected to the initiating identity across application and production system boundaries.
items.quantBasis: Sensitive actions with end to end attribution and forensic hours spent reconstructing actor identity.

phases.label: Govern
phases.value: One control plane for every application and agent, with enforceable policies, named ownership, complete audit history, controlled production access, and attributable spending.
phases.riskMitigated: Prevents decentralized development from becoming shadow IT with unknown owners, uncontrolled costs, inconsistent policies, and no reliable way to contain risk.

items.title: One inventory connects every asset to its owner and operating record
items.today: Tools are distributed across laptops, personal accounts, and unrelated hosts without one inventory or owner of record.
items.problem: Security, procurement, and IT cannot govern assets they cannot find.
items.impact: Unknown applications retain access, cost money, and survive owner changes, making the total exposure impossible to approve or contain.
items.withVercel: One inventory connects every application and agent to an owner, team, source, deployment, and operating record.
items.quantBasis: Unregistered applications discovered; share with named owner, data classification, and source lineage; inventory hours avoided.

items.title: Layered controls reduce the risk of excessive bills
items.today: Application, infrastructure, and AI usage grow without one consistent set of visibility, alerting, traffic, and response controls.
items.problem: Self-built safeguards vary by application, so abnormal consumption may continue until an owner or central team notices and intervenes.
items.impact: Traffic spikes, automated loops, abusive requests, or unexpected AI usage can create excessive bills and force broad restrictions on otherwise useful workloads.
items.withVercel: Vercel combines spend visibility, alerts, automated responses, AI usage reporting, inbound traffic controls, and restricted agent or sandbox egress to reduce the chance that abnormal usage becomes an uncontrolled bill.
items.quantBasis: Unexpected spend events; time from anomaly to action; abusive requests blocked; restricted outbound calls; spend attribution; and reconciliation hours.

items.title: Ingress and sandbox egress controls contain runaway or abusive traffic
items.today: Each self-hosted application must implement its own inbound abuse controls and rate limits, while agent or untrusted-code execution needs a separate outbound network policy.
items.problem: Application code becomes the last line of defense: malicious requests and software loops can reach compute or paid APIs before a limit runs, while unrestricted sandbox egress can call any external destination.
items.impact: A denial-of-service event, credential abuse, runaway retry loop, or compromised workload can multiply compute, data-transfer, model, and third-party API costs before an operator intervenes.
items.withVercel: Vercel WAF filters, denies, challenges, and rate-limits incoming requests at the edge; Vercel Sandbox policies can deny all egress or allowlist specific domains and network ranges before untrusted code or agents run.
items.quantBasis: Requests blocked before application resources; rate-limit events; outbound destinations denied; and compute, model, data-transfer, or third-party API calls avoided during abusive or runaway activity.

items.title: One audit chain connects identity, code, deployment, and activity
items.today: Identity, code changes, deployments, and production activity are logged in separate tools or not logged consistently.
items.problem: There is no complete chain from a named person to the code, release, and production action.
items.impact: Audit preparation becomes an investigation, while missing evidence expands incident scope, response time, and legal uncertainty.
items.withVercel: Identity, source, deployment, and production activity form one exportable record for internal security systems.
items.quantBasis: Measured from audit requests and evidence collection hours. Required events available centrally; incident scoping time.

items.title: Governed run records make agent actions reviewable and containable
items.today: Agents can query data, send messages, and change external systems without one record of trigger, tool calls, approvals, cost, and outcome.
items.problem: Machine speed actions lack the evidence needed to distinguish intended automation from unauthorized behavior.
items.impact: An error can propagate across systems before detection, and investigators must treat every connected system as affected.
items.withVercel: Each run records the initiating identity, trigger, actions, approvals, cost, and outcome for review and containment.
items.quantBasis: Agent runs with complete trace and named approval; time to reconstruct a failed run; systems touched per incident.

phases.label: Maintain
phases.value: Operate thousands of applications and agents as one managed fleet, with standardized operations, centralized visibility, platform updates, clear ownership, and enterprise support.
phases.riskMitigated: Prevents each application from becoming a separate operational liability with its own infrastructure, dependencies, security updates, expertise, and support burden.

items.title: One managed fleet absorbs platform maintenance across the estate
items.today: Self managed applications require capacity planning, runtime patching, cluster maintenance, upgrades, and deployment tooling.
items.problem: Operations grow with application count even when business usage does not.
items.impact: Each successful application adds permanent platform work until maintenance requires more specialists or new development is restricted.
items.withVercel: One managed fleet absorbs capacity, runtime, patching, and platform maintenance across the entire application estate.
items.quantBasis: Platform engineering effort per unit of estate, annual patch and upgrade hours, and incidents caused by platform maintenance rather than by the applications themselves.

items.title: Standard structure and company-owned source make ownership transferable
items.today: Business teams adopt applications whose source, knowledge, and operating context remain with the original builder.
items.problem: Adoption turns a personal project into business infrastructure without creating transferable ownership.
items.impact: When the builder changes role, the application degrades and the dependent process becomes an emergency handover.
items.withVercel: Company owned source, standard structure, explicit ownership, and common operations let another team take over.
items.quantBasis: Adopted applications without a secondary owner; business hours lost after owner departure; takeover effort per application.

items.title: Default telemetry shortens diagnosis before specialist escalation
items.today: Logs and traces are missing, fragmented, or accessible only to specialists.
items.problem: The person closest to the workflow cannot distinguish code, data access, external system, and infrastructure failures.
items.impact: Every incident enters a specialist queue and begins with reproduction while the business process remains unavailable.
items.withVercel: Default telemetry and one operating model let builders diagnose more failures before escalating them.
items.quantBasis: Measured from incident count and the time to first diagnosis and resolution. Specialist escalations avoided; share resolved with default telemetry.

items.title: Enterprise support absorbs platform questions as adoption grows
items.today: A small internal team becomes the help desk for every build, deployment, access, and incident question.
items.problem: Support grows with applications and builders, including questions about the underlying platform.
items.impact: Rollout is limited by internal support capacity or displaces governance, security, and platform work.
items.withVercel: Enterprise support absorbs platform questions while the internal team retains policy, business context, and escalation ownership.
items.quantBasis: Support tickets per unit of estate, handling time, loaded support rate, and the share resolved without internal platform intervention.

items.title: Portfolio visibility supports improvement, transfer, and retirement
items.today: After release, usage, ownership, and operating health are not visible across the portfolio.
items.problem: Valuable, failing, and abandoned applications look the same to central teams.
items.impact: The company funds unused tools, retains unnecessary access, and discovers ownerless applications only during incidents or audits.
items.withVercel: Portfolio level usage, cost, health, and ownership data supports targeted improvement, transfer, or retirement.
items.quantBasis: Active users, cost per active user, ownerless applications, and applications retired below an agreed usage threshold.
